q-106755.name: Question 1
q-106755.problem:
Which of the following products is the LU factorization of a matrix $A?$

I. $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -9 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]$

II. $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 5 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}7 & 0 \\ 0 & 8\end{aligned}]$

III. $A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 6 & 1\end{aligned}]$
q-106755.worked_solution:
Remember that in the LU factorization of a matrix $A,$ we write $A=LU$ where the matrix $L$ is a unit lower triangular matrix (a lower triangular matrix that has only $1$'s on the main diagonal) and the matrix $U$ is an upper triangular matrix:

$$
A=\overset{L}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ ∗ & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot \overset{U}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}∗ & ∗ \\ 0 & ∗\end{aligned}]}}
$$

With that in mind, let's inspect each product in turn.

- The first product is in $LU$ form because the left matrix is a unit lower triangular matrix, and the right matrix is an upper triangular matrix.

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -9 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\,✓
$$

- The second product is in $LU$ form because the left matrix is a unit lower triangular matrix, and the right matrix is an upper triangular matrix.

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 5 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}7 & 0 \\ 0 & 8\end{aligned}]\,✓
$$

- The third product is *not* in $LU$ form. Although we have a product of an upper triangular matrix on the left and a unit lower triangular matrix on the right, the order of multiplication is not correct (instead, we need a unit lower triangular matrix on the left and an upper triangular matrix on the right).

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 6 & 1\end{aligned}]\,\times 
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only".

q-106765.name: Question 6
q-106765.problem:
Given that 
$A=[\begin{aligned}-7 & 3 \\ 14 & -5\end{aligned}]$ 
has the LU decomposition $A=LU,$ then $L=$
q-106765.worked_solution:
To find the matrices $L$ and $U,$ we reduce the matrix $A$ to row echelon form. Whilst doing this, we simultaneously write down the row operations applied to $A$ in terms of matrix multiplication using elementary matrices:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}-7 & 3 \\ 14 & -5\end{aligned}] & \,{R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1}\,⟺\,\overset{{E}_{1}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot A \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-7 & 3 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =U\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix $U.$ Now, since ${E}_{1}A=U,$ we can invert ${E}_{1}$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{1}A & =U \\ A & ={E}_{1}^{-1}U \\ A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ A & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}{{[\begin{aligned}-7 & 3 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{U}\end{aligned}
$$

q-32617.problem:
Given that 
$B=[\begin{aligned}3 & 9 \\ 7 & 20\end{aligned}]$ 
has the LU decomposition $B=LU$, then ${l}_{21}\cdot {u}_{12}=$
q-32617.worked_solution:
To find the matrices $L$ and $U,$ we reduce the matrix $B$ to row echelon form. Whilst doing this, we simultaneously write down the row operations applied to $B$ in terms of matrix multiplication using elementary matrices:

$$
\begin{aligned}B & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 9 \\ 7 & 20\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-\frac{7}{3}){R}_{1}\,⟺\,\overset{{E}_{1}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -\frac{7}{3} & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot B \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}3 & 9 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =U\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix $U.$ Now, since ${E}_{1}B=U,$ we can invert ${E}_{1}$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{1}B & =U \\ B & ={E}_{1}^{-1}U \\ B & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -\frac{7}{3} & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ B & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ \frac{7}{3} & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}{{[\begin{aligned}3 & 9 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{U}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${l}_{21}=\frac{7}{3},{u}_{12}=9,$ and ${l}_{21}\cdot {u}_{12}=21.$

To find the matrices $L$ and $U,$ we reduce the matrix $A$ to row echelon form. Whilst doing this, we simultaneously write down the row operations applied to $A$ in terms of matrix multiplication using elementary matrices:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 7 & 9\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-7){R}_{1}\,⟺\,\overset{{E}_{1}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -7 & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot A \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 0 & -5\end{aligned}] \\  & =U\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix $U.$ Now, since ${E}_{1}A=U,$ we can invert ${E}_{1}$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{1}A & =U \\ A & ={E}_{1}^{-1}U \\ A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -7 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ A & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 7 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}{{[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 0 & -5\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{U}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${l}_{21}=7,{u}_{22}=-5,$ and ${l}_{21}\cdot {u}_{12}=-35.$

q-32545.problem:
Given that
$A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ -6 & -4\end{aligned}]$
has the LU decomposition $A=LU$, then ${l}_{21}+{u}_{22}=$
q-32545.worked_solution:
To find the matrices $L$ and $U,$ we reduce the matrix $A$ to row echelon form. Whilst doing this, we simultaneously write down the row operations applied to $A$ in terms of matrix multiplication using elementary matrices:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ -6 & -4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1}\,⟺\,\overset{{E}_{1}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot A \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =U\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix $U.$ Now, since ${E}_{1}A=U,$ we can invert ${E}_{1}$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{1}A & =U \\ A & ={E}_{1}^{-1}U \\ A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ A & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}{{[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{U}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${l}_{21}=-2,$ ${u}_{22}=0,$ and ${l}_{21}+{u}_{22}=-2.$

Given that A=[−2−8−1−4] has the LU decomposition A=LU, then l21+u22=

a
0
b
2
c
1
d

e
12

Correct
EXPLANATION

To find the matrices L and U, we reduce the matrix A to row echelon form. Whilst doing this, we simultaneously write down the row operations applied to A in terms of matrix multiplication using elementary matrices:

A=[−2−8−1−4]R2:=R2+(−12)R1⟺[10−121]⏞E1⋅A∼[−2−800]=U

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix U. Now, since E1A=U, we can invert E1 to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

E1A=UA=E1−1UA=[10−121]−1UA=[10121]⏟L[−2−800]⏟U

Therefore, l21=12, u22=0, and l21+u22=12.

q-75177.problem:
Given that
$A=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 \\ 1 & \,\,\,-\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}]$
has the LU decomposition $A=LU$, then ${l}_{21}+{u}_{22}=$
q-75177.worked_solution:
To find the matrices $L$ and $U,$ we reduce the matrix $A$ to row echelon form. Whilst doing this, we simultaneously write down the row operations applied to $A$ in terms of matrix multiplication using elementary matrices:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 \\ 1 & \,\,\,-\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1}\,⟺\,\overset{{E}_{1}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ \frac{1}{2} & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot A \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =U\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix $U.$ Now, since ${E}_{1}A=U,$ we can invert ${E}_{1}$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{1}A & =U \\ A & ={E}_{1}^{-1}U \\ A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ \frac{1}{2} & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ A & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -\frac{1}{2} & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}{{[\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{U}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${l}_{21}=-\frac{1}{2},$ ${u}_{22}=0,$ and ${l}_{21}+{u}_{22}=-\frac{1}{2}.$
